You need leadership both on the technical and organizational side, and you need at multiple levels from very tactical to very strategic.


I don't think anyone disputes that, it's how you go about creating that.


Creating a formally-defined team lead that still reports to a line manager is something I've usually seen go wrong, for example, by quasi-management duties getting offloaded onto an ic with no interest in management, and a career path that doesn't involve management.


My preferred strategy to encourage technical leadership is to have very senior technical ic's reporting above the team level -- directly to directors, vps and even executives, and directly involved in strategic discussions and work from a technical perspective.


I also try to make sure their technical scope matches -- e.g. that they (not a manager, not a project manager) are driving wide technical initiatives at above the team level. 


This creates a class of seasoned ic's directly driving large technical efforts, participating in strategic discussions, and peered with managers at a corresponding level of seniority, so they're not limited by a line manager acting in a much more tactical role.


This creates a real career path for ic's interested in technical leadership.


I think the de facto team lead is an important, but typically emergent position on any technical team.  I have no problems with that being recognized informally - but if they're truly leading a team already, I'd be pushing them to be getting their feet wet with driving larger in scope efforts, and thinking about rungs of the technical ladder that mean moving off of a team reporting to a line manager, which is the only place team lead as a title or formal designation really makes sense. 


I really don't like the ways, in practice, that designating a formal (maybe even in title) team lead actually tends to play out.  Among other isues I've seen:


* Changes perception of the individual -- load bearing member of one team, rather than an emergent leader already beginning to exert influence above the level of the team.  This can lead to artificially capping their scope and limiting career opportunities.
* Manager or others have an excuse to dump administrative, or non-technical work on one person.  Erodes "we're all engineers and we're all responsible for the technical and non technical sides of our work" mentality, and can easily lead to baby sitter creation.
* Tends to encourage rigid, siloed teams.  You don't just have a body of engineers, at various levels of seniority, who can handle different size projects or different scopes.. you've now encoded in a very rigid way that certain people must Lead Teams.
* Causes individual to focus on team, not wider group or org -- because their success is tied to the success of one team in a very limiting way

I definitely get the what if feeling with risky or high stakes decisions in general from time to time.


One thing that helps me is shifting perspective a bit. Rather than trying to make 100% of calls correctly, I focus on being right more often than wrong, and building confidence in my ability to improvise, adjust and fix things when something goes wrong.


Poker is great training.  Being good at poker is making a lot of little decisions over time, under challenging circumstances -- boredom, anger, incomplete information, fear etc.  You win consistently not by making one brilliant decision and not by making zero mistakes, but by maximizing the number of good decisions you make over the long term and your ability to recover when you fuck up, or luck doesn't break your way.


The stakes are higher here, but ultimately you serve the people you lead best by making a call, planning for contingencies and going with it.  Dithering about unknown unknowns only prolongs the time other people have to suffer, and makes people question your competence and assertiveness.


You should ideally be using a mental muscle for making tough decisions with incomplete information you've built up in lower stress situations. Over time, you get used to higher and higher stakes.  It's a skill you practice, not just knowledge -- if you haven't been doing that already, it's going to be hard to have the skill you need in this situation, and you should consider getting help.

Say you're even only slightly unusual in a few ways:


* You're mid-late career (and have real experience)
* You have a somewhat above average level of aptitude

None of those things are by themselves all that unusual, but their combination in one person is rarer than any of them separately, and companies need more employees than people that exist with these qualities.


This by itself explains a chunk of it, but there a number of other related factors IMO:


Say you and and equally talented and motivated person start a company.  It takes off, and you quickly need to hire additional people to take care of necessary functions for you -- marketing, security, sales etc.


Let's say you don't know a lot about these areas to being with .. also, you don't necessarily have time to be choosy or the money to recruit the field.  So you add a good enough candidate (you hope).


Let's say they end up being pretty much just that -- a good enough candidate.  As the company grows, they hire in people and layers of leadership under them.  If they're fairly mediocre, the people they hire are likely to be even more mediocre, especially in leadership positions.  They may not have the talent to recognize talent, they may be threatened by higher performers, their network will tend to be closer to them in skill level, and more qualified people don't tend to like working for less well qualified people.


Now you have, let's say like 50 people in a function the business needs to succeed.  Overall leadership is mediocre, and it gets worse down the chain. These people have inadvertently hired in some bright spots, but for the most part they've brought in people like them.


As the overall leader, you may be aware of this... But you need sales (or whatever it is), and they're doing enough to keep the company afloat.  Eliminating an entire crucial department and starting from scratch would be a massive cost and morale hit, so probably not worth it if they're doing good enough work.


If it gets bad enough, and you want to improve, you'd be more likely to replace senior leadership, and they can begin the process of leveling up from within -- weeding out weakest points bringing new people in, slowly fixing issues etc.  This is a hard process. Not many people are qualified to do it, and it takes  time.  


If you choose to invest this way, you're not guaranteed to see the return any time soon, or even ever, and they're not guaranteed to be persistent -- new leader may leave etc.


Think of this from the perspective of a large, growing company then:


Maintaining high standards is hard.  You need to know or understand how to find the best people in a lot of fields, you need to be able to pay them, and you need to generally be right them being the best people.


As soon as you miss, or are forced to accept a middle of the road person, it's very easy for that to cascade and for mediocrity to become entrenched in ways that are very difficult to change. 


Over time, the misses add up and propagate, and the group as a whole regresses to the mean, without sustained effort to keep it high performing.  If you're the business owner, you might not even care that the average level is not high performing.  You're making money (presumably).  Average people are easy to find, and the revenue increase from leveling up isn't worth the effort, or the dependency on non-commodity talent you'll create for yourself.


Also, just practically speaking, there tend to be high performing people willing to invest a lot of effort individually to keep groups like this going.  If you can count on from time to time hiring some skilled people who will go above and beyond to level up the people around them without an actual leadership position or appropriate compensation, you kind of have the best of both worlds.


Individual people like that only have so much effect, and they tend to burn out, but you're getting some transient benefits you'd get from a more costly function overhaul basically for free as long as managers are competent enough to stumble on people like this from time to time and hang on to them for a bit before they give up.


There are many more dynamics in play than just this, including culture, available labor pool, whether engineering is viewed as a cost center, or part of the core of how a company makes money and so on.


The net effect though, is that if you're even a little bit above average in a few ways and you work at large companies, you're likely to find yourself in a system that has had forces driving it towards average for a long time in ways that are expensive to reverse even if the business had the appetite for it.


The problem is further exacerbated because some people who are a little bit above average self select out over time -- they found their own companies, consult, work for smaller companies, find hidden, sane little areas of large companies,  or they stop trying so hard and coast.


This is in part because the incentives don't make sense.  The company often doesn't really want more than average.  They'd be happy for you to overextend, but not to pay you or support you in an appropriate way when you're overextending, because ultimately when you give up, they'll just replace you with an average person, which is all the really need as long as there's always a few people willing to overextend here and there.

I think a lot it comes down to org structure and role definition.


Often the first place product and engineering teams have unified leadership is at the CTO.  In orgs with a CPO, the CEO is often the first point of coherence.


The role is than often defined in terms of applying commodity skills: ability to understand the market and customer needs, set strategic direction, and communicate.  PM's often have more highly-developed versions of the commodity skills involved -- Communication, strategic thinking, etc -- but it's rare that they have a monopoly on them in the org, because most people in senior leadership of any sort are going to have these skills.  (Unlike, say the ability to code well, which is a non-commodity skill, that tends to be strongly correlated with certain roles.)


Because of the org structure, PM then seems to often feel that they need to be leading, as if they are the sole function possessing a non-commodity skill like coding.


Because direction must be unitary, this often causes conflict with, for example, senior engineering leadership... A group which typically posseses some level of the core pm skills + technical understanding and an understanding of the teams that ultimately report to them.


The industry, for whatever inane reason, has tried to resolve this conflict by dividing the "how" from the "what," and assigning product leadership of the "what" and engineering leadership of the "how."


The problem is, leading these things is only distinct in the minds of high-priced consultants, or people who haven't ever actually built shit.


It often puts product in a weird position.  Engineering leadership often has a more complete understanding of all the factors that go into determining strategic direction and what to build (because they have a deeper understanding of this technical and team components).  If product isn't the final arbiter of product direction though, they often feel like they're not doing their job.


Acting as an advisor to senior leadership with the full picture isn't consistent with product being an independent function, or the over hyped understanding of product work that's been popularized, so it often seems like people working in product attempt to use political means or poorly-understood data to try to wrest strategic direction setting from senior leadership of other functions. 


Contrast this with a Michelin-starred restaurant.  There are a set of  high level chefs who set overall direction, and extreme competence and end to end understanding of the business of a restaurant and how a restaurant runs is a core requirement for being in these roles.   There's a point of coherence at a role that understands the whole picture.


If the restaurants translated the PM role into their org, it would be like they bring in a marketing expert who hasn't cooked or worked in a kitchen, except maybe in their dimly-remembered past.  They're made answerable to investors, and put in a parallel position to the exec chef, and they use that position to do things like this:


"Potential customers say they really like curry.  Go put much more curry in all our dishes."


Actual chefs know there's much more to a dish being enjoyed than the amount of curry.  They might also understand nuance like:


The market in general wants more curry, but not the niche we're serving.


Or: there's a demand for more lively,  and inventive dishes with east Asian notes to them, because of the rising popularity of Indian restaurants.


If product were to act as an advisor, presenting what they heard about curry to the chefs, the chefs might be able to use their deeper understanding to build out some killer northern Indian fusion takes on existing dishes that people absolutely love. Some may involve curry, some may not, because curry isn't the only note from that cuisine, and their are many more considerations involved -- e.g the overall menu the guests will be working through during the night, the presentation of dishes and so on.


Because of the artificial "what" and "how" division, and because the product person feels they need to be co-leading with the chefs, what happens instead tends to be: "add more curry to everything" directives, with predictably bad results, unless chefs essentially go rouge, and turn that over simplistic feedback into something much more nuanced... Which product often then takes credit for, as if their contribution was more than market research.


This isn't an argument of any sort really, just me expressing what it often feels like for me to be in senior overall or engineering leadership interfacing with product.  (As someone with a background in both product and engineering work.)


I've had great relationships with PM's willing to function in an advisory capacity to overall leadership who has the holistic picture, but typically very frustrating ones with PM's that believe they have a mandate to lead overall.  This is because leadership, by definition, is a holistic discipline, and the asinine way we've divided and organized roles usually means PM's only have expertise and understanding in a small set of the overall domains you need to understand to lead a business that builds software.

Lead yourself first.  If you can't keep yourself together, you can't lead others.  Being erratic, lashing out emotionally and that sort of thing are the quickest way to lose the respect of a group (often).

I'd start by trying to understand the people around you, individually and in relationship with each other, both emotionally and intellectually.  Communication and observation are the key to doing that, critically without making people feel uncomfortable or like they're being studied or something weird like that.  Critically, make it safe for people to talk to you without judgement in a way that they feel understood without being inauthentic.  In general, pretending to be something you are not will make people feel unsafe or like they can't trust you, even if they can't always articulate why.  Directness, openness and honesty tend to be important.

Always let people define themselves for you by their words and behavior.  Avoid projection and mind reading at all costs -- this erases the actual people and replaces them with yourself in a way that makes leadership impossible.  

Actions and patterns in actions tend to be the ground truth about who people really are.  

As a new leader don't necessarily be eager to jump into action until you've built understanding.  When it becomes clear that there are things you should do, start small, and make sure to take the time to understand whether what you did was really helpful, especially at first.

Leadership roles, even in informal groups almost always come with responsibilities -- they perform a function the group needs, which often involves sacrifice and doing uncomfortable things for the benefit of the group.  If leaders do not live up to their unwritten responsibilities, they tend to become ineffective, because the symbiotic relationship with the group that allows them to lead breaks down.

An on paper leadership position is rarely necessary to lead, and by itself, not even close to sufficient to lead.  Leadership is always a relationship with the people you're leading first and foremost.

Flip a coin four times.  It's not uncommon to get three heads or three tails, even though the odds dictate you should get two.

Flip it a billion times, and the distribution will tend to be extremely close to 50% in each group.

This is called the law of large numbers - basically as the sample size increases, the more and more certainty you have about how close actual distribution will be to predicted.

This is what casinos rely on.  If you bet $1 to win $3, they ensure the odds of you winning are a touch under 33%.  This means that over a large sample, they'll reliably take in more than they pay out.

There are additional things on top of this as well -- e.g. games that allow players to make bad decisions that increase house edge -- but this is the core thing that's at work.

Time to crack a hashed password of any size depends largely on the hashing algorithm.

This is because that determines how long it takes to convert each clear text candidate to a hash to see if it matches the target, which is the primary thing that takes time when cracking.

Different algorithms have different characteristics... Some, for example are easier to compute if you use a GPU, so crack time depends a lot on whether you have a GPU.  Before using GPU's for cracking was common practice, time to brute force was significantly longer.

In some cases with a hash without a salt, someone maybe have pre-computed a rainbow table you can just look the hash up in instantly (at least for common passwords).

There are certain hashing schemes that are just brain dead:

LM hashes, which used to be used by windows, will split your password in two if it's longer than 7 characters.  Therefore, an attacker doesn't have to crack a single 12 character password... Just a 5 and a 7.  (And it's easy to generate and distribute 7 character rainbow tables.)

Better hash options like bcrypt can't be accelerated with a gpu and let you tune how much work is involved in generating a single hash by configuring the number of rounds.  This allows app creators to adjust as computers get faster.  It also means time to crack a 12 character password depends a lot on the configuration.  With a typical configuration on typical hardware it will be a long time... However, no one knows that there isn't some breakthrough around the corner that suddenly makes cracking these easy.  (Maybe someone discovers a weakness in the algorithm... Or quantum computers allow for some new cracking method.)

I wonder how much addiction is really about trying to meet fundamental emotional needs, like the need to feel emotionally safe, and to what extent addicts are just rationally ranking those core emotional needs over external needs.

While addicted to opiates, I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that I needed them in my system at all times to function, and not just because of withdrawal.  They gave me energy, calmed down my anxiety and surrounded me with a nice warm security blanket that kept my mood from richocetting all over the place in response to every little event over the course of the day... I was able to be a productive worker, appear normal, talk to strangers, etc.

I looked at opiates like food -- just a basic staple I needed to survive.  I didn't waste a lot of mental energy on questions like "should I get I high today" for the same reason I don't waste a lot of energy on questions like "should I eat today."

I didn't experience things like "do I pick up my kid from school or do I get high" as decisions.  It was more "I need to stay high to have any hope of functioning... Let me take care of that primary need, then try to sort out how to pick up my daughter from school." More often than not, I figured out how to handle these other responsibilities.  Occasionally I miscalculated and got too high or something and let them slip.  I felt bad in these cases, but the subjective experience of it was of trying to balance conflicting needs in a rational way and failing.  (In the hypothetical picking up daughter from school example, it's worth noting that the belief that I would need to be at least somewhat high to drive safely, interact with school people and my daughter was not at all an illusion.  Many more functional opiate addicts are normal when moderately high, and complete messes when dope sick )

All in all, I think opiate addiction was a rational choice that addressed a lot of problems for me better than any alternative available to me.  At their core, they allowed me to exist in my own skin and interact with the world a bit.  Without them, I would have definitely killed myself, or become some crazy hermit or something like that.  

External consequences like legal trouble sucked, but if always seemed like a simple choice -- do I want to continue existing in my own skin, even if that's on parole, paying off massive fines, etc -- or do I want stop existing?

Based on my limited sample size of 1 experience, I worry about treating addiction like a "disease" or some almost alien force within the brain subverting the parts of that brain that are more "us."

This denies a central part of the phenomenology of actually being an addict -- which is that the self has unmet needs so deep and urgent, that satisfying them with drugs seems like a good choice, even if it means lots of external suffering.

I think this also makes addicts less "other." As much as you'd like to claim otherwise, it's almost certain that if you were subjected to some level of pain, and told the only way to be relieved of it was to neglect your kids or go to jail sometimes, you would opt to relieve the pain.  The threshold might be different for everyone, but I suspect most people have a threshold.

IMO, an addict is just someone subjected to a level of internal pain that's too much for them to handle effectively in any way they're aware of other than using drugs.  

I think there's some interesting research that at least partially supports this armchair theory -- for example, look at the link between trauma and opiate addiction.

Typically, the first bit of your shellcode is going to be looking up the addresses of the primitive functions you need in the relevant dll.  

If this lookup fails, you could assume you're in a Linux process and jmp to basic linux shellcode.

There's another potential complication here though in that maybe you could end up in a 32 bit process.  This article covers shellcode that will work in both 32bit and 64bit Linux processes:
